The strongest argument for a three-fund hold-forever portfolio is behavioral, not mathematical. The simpler the portfolio, the less tempted you are to tinker at exactly the moments tinkering hurts most, which for FIRE matters because the early withdrawal years are when sequence risk and panic-selling do the real damage. In my view the one thing a three-ETF plan still has to solve separately is the first few years of withdrawals: hold-forever works beautifully until a bad sequence early in retirement forces selling shares to eat. A cash buffer bolted onto the simplicity covers the gap the three funds alone don't.

VUG and QQQM have 100% overlap with VTI since VTI is literally the entire US stock market. Buying VUG or QQQM just buy more of the same stocks, so you have a tilt. VIG has a 1.5% yield, plus growth but VTI has a 1% yield and more growth - over the last 5 years VTI has outperformed VIG by almost 3% per year, which is a lot more than that 0.5% yield per year. My plan is 80% VTI, 20% VXUS (because you never know) and then hold 3 years of expected living expenses at retirement in VBIL. Pull living expenses from VBIL when the market crashes, refill it when it's up. Calculate your target yearly retirement expense first and divide that by 8% and that is your target for VTI + VXUS. Then ask AI to calculate how much you need to save each month into all three. If I want 10K pretax (capital gains) per month in retirement and I retire in 20 years, I need to put $1890 into VTI, $470 into VXUS, plus $1,000 into VBIL each month. With the goal of maintaining that 1.5m until I die, leaving it to my kids. So that's $3,360 a month. Maybe we can collect social security too, if it's still around.

The strongest argument for a three-fund hold-forever portfolio is behavioral, not mathematical. The simpler the portfolio, the less tempted you are to tinker at exactly the moments tinkering hurts most, which for FIRE matters because the early withdrawal years are when sequence risk and panic-selling do the real damage. In my view the one thing a three-ETF plan still has to solve separately is the first few years of withdrawals: hold-forever works beautifully until a bad sequence early in retirement forces selling shares to eat. A cash buffer bolted onto the simplicity covers the gap the three funds alone don't.
